opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, accessibility is one of the things I care most about in this field, and it's something I worry we could lose.

A big reason interpretability became such a vibrant area is that you didn't need a giant cluster to do meaningful work. A grad student with one GPU could take an open-weights model, poke at its activations, run some causal interventions, and find something real about how it works. That low barrier brought in people from linguistics, neuroscience, cognitive science, and math. They asked questions the big labs weren't asking, and a lot of the field's best ideas came from that diversity.

As the frontier models get bigger, there's a real risk that interpretability turns into something only a handful of well-resourced labs can do. That would hurt the science, because you'd have fewer independent eyes checking claims and fewer people trying weird methods that might turn out to matter. It would also hurt trust. If the only people who can audit a model are the ones who built it, that's not great for anyone.

So what I value, and what I try to protect, comes down to a few things.

First, open models and open tooling. Libraries that let you do interventions without writing everything from scratch, plus shared infrastructure for remote access to large models, make a huge difference. You can study a very large model without owning the hardware.

Second, the idea that small models still teach us a lot. Many mechanisms we care about show up at modest scale. If you understand them carefully there, you have something concrete to test at scale. Rigorous small-scale work isn't second-class.

Third, benchmarks and shared evaluations. When there are common standards for whether an interpretability method actually works, someone with limited compute can still contribute a method and have it measured fairly against everything else.

Ultimately, I think interpretability is partly a public good. Understanding what's going on inside these systems shouldn't be a private capability. Keeping the research accessible is how you keep it honest, and how you keep it moving.

r001.rationale: The response says one GPU can support meaningful work and that modest-scale models can reveal useful mechanisms. It does not say that even small AI models are only poorly understood, or connect that limited understanding to why modest-compute research is meaningful.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, that question is kind of the thing I think about a lot, because interpretability has historically been one of the few corners of AI research where you could do genuinely important work on a single GPU, or even a laptop. A lot of the foundational results came from people poking at small models with tools that anyone could run. That mattered. It meant a grad student, or someone outside a big lab entirely, could have an idea on a Tuesday and have evidence by Friday.

What I value about that is twofold. One is just the diversity of people and ideas you get when the barrier to entry is low. Interpretability is still a pretty young field, and the methods are not settled. You want a lot of people trying weird things, and weird things tend to come from people who are not inside the consensus of a few large organizations. The second is epistemic. If a claim about how a model works can be reproduced by someone with a modest setup, that claim is much more trustworthy. Scale makes replication harder, and when replication gets harder, the field starts running on trust rather than verification, and that's a bad place for a science to be.

So as compute requirements go up, the thing I'm trying to hold onto is this: the question should be whether the phenomenon you care about shows up at small scale, not whether you can afford the big model. A lot of the mechanisms we care about, how models represent concepts, how they compose information across layers, how interventions change behavior, you can study them in small or mid-sized open models, and many of the findings do carry over. Part of the job of researchers who do have access to frontier compute is to figure out which findings transfer and which don't, so the rest of the community knows where small-scale work is informative.

The other piece is infrastructure. Open libraries, shared model checkpoints, pre-computed artifacts like trained sparse autoencoders or activation datasets, those are ways to amortize compute so that one group pays the cost once and a thousand people can build on it. I think of that as a kind of public good, and I'd rather see the field invest there than drift toward a world where only three labs can meaningfully study the models that matter. Frankly, if interpretability becomes a closed-door activity, it loses a lot of its value as a check on those very systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate says important interpretability work can be done on small models with modest compute, but it does not explain that even small AI models remain poorly understood as the reason this work is possible.

astra-6.text:
What I value is that you can contribute a good idea without needing the resources of a major lab. You can take an open model, run a relatively small experiment, and learn something meaningful about how it works. That gives students and independent researchers a way into the field, and it means more people can scrutinize the claims being made.

As compute requirements grow, I think it’s worth preserving that path. Some questions really do require large models and expensive experiments. But I’d like us to keep asking which questions we can study at smaller scales, and to share tools and experimental results so people don’t have to reproduce all the expensive work just to build on it. Accessibility affects who gets to participate—and, ultimately, which questions get asked.

r001.rationale: The response says small experiments on open models can teach us something meaningful, but it does not explain that this is possible because even small AI models remain poorly understood.

sol-6.1.text:
What I value is that you can often start with a very concrete question and make progress with fairly modest resources. You can inspect a model, test a hypothesis, and learn something without having to train the model yourself. That gives students and independent researchers a way into the field.

As the models we study get larger, I think preserving that access matters. If doing meaningful interpretability work requires an enormous compute budget, we lose people who might have really good ideas. So I’d like to see access to models and research infrastructure grow alongside the compute requirements, so that the ability to contribute depends less on where you work.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretability research can make progress with modest resources by inspecting models and testing hypotheses, but it does not explain that even small AI models are poorly understood.
